Narrator: Enquiries on a hot air balloon trip.

Agent: A single ride may cost you up to 280 pounds per person. But if you choose a group booking there is a discount, and the cheapest flight is 125 pounds each for a group booking of at least ten people.

Agent: Upon completing the trip we will provide each participant with a certificate, and that is entirely free of charge.

Agent: Reservations can be made one year ahead of your trip by telephone, but to pick a specific date you must book online. A confirmation e-mail will be sent to you right afterwards.

Agent: A hot air balloon's height is limited by the temperature of the air and how much fuel it can carry, and the highest altitude ever recorded for a ride is 1800 metres. Most rides stay below 300 metres.

Agent: Our flights generally meet about an hour before sunrise on the day, and you will be notified of the exact meeting time the evening before your flight. Night flights are avoided because of the weather conditions.

Agent: Autumn is the best time of year to take the trip. Not only can you see the changing hues of the trees from above, but it is a great way to spend time with the whole family before it gets too cold.

Agent: It can be quite dangerous to fly in bad weather conditions, like a thunderstorm, so our experienced pilots will not go up in such conditions.

Agent: We suggest wearing comfortable clothing like a jacket — multiple layers are always better. Wearing a helmet for safety is also a good idea. Sandals are not permitted.

Agent: All children must be above the minimum age of nine years old and they have to be accompanied by at least a parent or guardian. However, an adult has no age limit as long as they meet the health requirements.

Agent: They must also be able to stand unassisted for an hour during the flight — it is the required position for the whole flight.

Narrator: Rivermead School: facilities open to the public.

Speaker: I'd like to start by talking about the new theatre that we've just opened in our school. Its mission is to maximise opportunities for local audiences to experience productions of the highest quality.

Speaker: As well as music and dance there'll be drama from modern writers, and there'll also be a high proportion of shows aimed at children and families. You'll notice that there is one empty space in November — that's because the Chinese state acrobatic troupe have had to cancel their visit.

Speaker: Now, we're often asked about the theatre's sources of funding. Well, a limited amount of money will come from various government subsidies, but the bulk of the revenue will be generated by the sale of tickets, which is one reason why we'd be grateful for your help in promoting the work of the theatre.

Speaker: Entrance to the museum is free. We also have a state-of-the-art sports hall. This is reserved for our students during term time, but anyone can use it in the school holidays. And our cafeteria is worth a visit — it's open all day to visitors as well as to staff and students.

Speaker: First of all, the theatre — that's opposite car park P2, on the south side. You're not allowed to park anywhere except in the car parks.

Speaker: There are two marked on your map, P1 and P2, but there's a new car park which has only just been completed, and that's at the most northern end of the campus.

Speaker: Some people might want to consider coming by bus. There's a good service from the city centre to the school, and the bus stops at the roundabout — that's where it turns round to go back. It doesn't go up as far as Park Road.

Speaker: Then, to get to the sports hall you take the right fork after the main entrance and just keep going past the classroom block. You have to go straight across the roundabout, and it's further on, on the right-hand side of that road.

Speaker: Then there's the cafeteria. There are various ways to get there, because it's at the junction of Park Road and Rennie's Drive, on the north side of Park Road. In nice weather you can sit outside to eat and admire the view.

Speaker: Then the museum is fairly central. Just go left after the main entrance, take the first turning on the right, and when you reach a junction the museum is facing you.

Narrator: Peter and Lynne discuss Professor Smith's article on online learning.

Peter: When I read that article it was clear to me that Professor Smith does not favour the traditional methods of classroom teaching. I think it's about time to revolutionise the old teaching style, though.

Lynne: I would hope that students consider the negatives of online learning before enrolling in online courses.

Peter: Professor Smith points out that computer learning is well suited to some courses, especially the technical courses.

Lynne: Unfortunately, that theory doesn't work for me.

Peter: I think the personal interaction offered by traditional teaching is overrated in the article and doesn't have much value.

Lynne: Oh, I disagree strongly, Peter.

Peter: Online courses can foster students' technological skills — students will gain the technical know-how they'll need in their future endeavours.

Lynne: I can't agree more.

Lynne: What do you think Professor Smith means when he says online courses should be flexible in time?

Peter: That's essentially the point of learning online — to allow those who can't attend courses at a fixed time.

Lynne: I agree.

Peter: Well, I think what he's trying to say is that students are already accustomed to doing their research on the Internet, although some people say computers could be better used for other purposes.

Peter: Professor Smith probably intends to say that computers are not easily accessible and available to all students.

Lynne: With online courses the student support system is already in place. Instead of asking fellow students or the professor for assistance, students would be able to get any information they need online, and this assistance would be available immediately.

Lynne: I think it's all about the money — he is promoting online courses simply because he thinks it will enable the school to make more money.

Narrator: Technology and education.

Lecturer: Some people believed that the use of e-mail between students and teachers made them interact with each other less, and that this was not a good thing.

Lecturer: Moreover, there is a tight relationship with the local economy when it comes to the effectiveness of the use of IT in education.

Lecturer: The most common example of teachers using technology in education is the use of computers to develop their teaching methods — in most classrooms you can see teachers using computers to present teaching notes and other materials.

Lecturer: It involves a kind of software which allows students as well as teachers to talk and discuss with each other more easily, and they said they enjoy this way of communication.

Lecturer: So it gives them a chance to showcase their strengths and build up their confidence.

Lecturer: They don't have to wait all night trying to register for their favourite elective courses — compared with the traditional platform, it is more flexible.

Lecturer: By the way, all the materials are original works of teachers or scholars, so there is no need to worry about the quality of the content.

Lecturer: So this mode gives students a new search engine they can use on campus. This is a perfect example of new solutions to new problems.

Lecturer: Students can arrange their daily activities and improve their time management skills by simply ticking the boxes in the timetable online.

Lecturer: Another feature is that students can help people who have questions or problems relating to their field of study on a special platform. They can even earn some income by providing people with good solutions.
